DOCUMENT:
Menu Pricing Review: Spring 2026
The Copper Kettle, prepared by the General Manager for the owners, March 2026

1. Purpose
This paper reviews main-course pricing and menu mix and proposes changes to take effect with the spring menu on 1 April 2026. Our overall gross margin on food, across all courses, has slipped from 70% to 67% over the past year as ingredient costs have risen faster than our prices, and we last changed main-course prices in September 2024.

2. Trading pattern
The Copper Kettle is a 64-cover restaurant open for lunch and dinner from Wednesday to Sunday. We serve an average of 1,050 main courses a week, with Friday and Saturday dinner accounting for just under half. Our customers are mainly local, with a strong repeat base: our booking system shows that around 60% of bookings come from guests who have dined with us in the past six months.

Table 1. Main courses, average weekly sales (January-February 2026)
Dish | Menu price | Food cost per plate | Gross margin | Plates per week
Fish and chips | £16.50 | £5.10 | 69% | 310
Beef burger | £15.00 | £4.20 | 72% | 260
Chicken curry | £14.50 | £3.60 | 75% | 180
Sirloin steak | £26.00 | £10.40 | 60% | 120
Mushroom risotto | £14.00 | £2.80 | 80% | 90
Other mains (specials) | various | various | 64% | 90

3. Competitor prices
We checked menus at the five restaurants we regard as our closest competitors. Their fish and chips ranges from £16.95 to £19.00, burgers from £15.50 to £17.50 and sirloin steak from £27.00 to £32.00. Our prices for these three dishes are the lowest in the group.

4. Supplier costs
Our meat supplier has given notice that beef prices will rise by 12% from 1 April 2026, reflecting national cattle prices. Other supplier prices are expected to be broadly stable over the spring. Fish prices have been volatile but are currently close to their 2025 average.

5. Proposals
5.1 Price increases. Raise fish and chips to £17.50, the beef burger to £16.00 and the sirloin steak to £28.00. All three would remain below the midpoint of the competitor range for that dish.

5.2 Remove the mushroom risotto. Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place. We propose replacing it with a seasonal vegetarian special at the same price.

5.3 Projected effect. If volumes hold, the price increases add £1.00 per plate on 310 fish and chips, £1.00 on 260 burgers and £2.00 on 120 steaks, a total of £810 a week in additional gross profit, or £42,120 a year. Because our prices remain competitive and our customer base is loyal, we expect volumes to hold. The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target.

6. Communication
Menus will be reprinted for 1 April. Staff will be briefed on the changes, and we will not draw attention to the increases on the menu. We will monitor plates sold per dish weekly for the first eight weeks against the January to February baseline.

7. Risks
Some regular guests may notice the increases. However, the last price change in 2024 had no visible effect on bookings, and the new prices remain competitive. Weekday lunch trade is more price-sensitive than dinner, but it represents a small share of main-course sales.

8. Recommendation
We recommend that the owners approve the three price increases and the replacement of the mushroom risotto from 1 April 2026. Together these changes add about £42,000 a year in gross profit, improve our margin and keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [misread_evidence] at: "Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place." -- Table 1 shows mushroom risotto has the highest gross margin on the menu (80%); the weakest is sirloin steak (60%). Lowest sales is correct (90 plates, tied with specials), but the margin claim misreads the table.
2. [missing_consideration] at: "The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target." -- The projection uses current food costs, but section 4 states beef prices rise 12% from 1 April, the same date as the new prices. Burgers and steaks (380 plates a week) would see higher food costs (e.g. about £1.25 more per steak), eroding much of the projected gain; the margin and profit projections never account for it.
3. [inconsistency] at: "keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week" -- Section 2 says the restaurant is open Wednesday to Sunday, i.e. five days a week; the recommendation refers to six trading days.

REVIEW:
# Review: Menu Pricing Review, Spring 2026

**The till data, competitor check and price arithmetic are all sound. But two of the paper's main conclusions don't follow from its own figures.**

- **The risotto.** The mushroom risotto has the **highest** margin on the menu, at 80%, not the weakest. Replacing it would probably *reduce* gross profit.
- **The beef price rise.** The paper reports a 12% beef price rise from 1 April, the same day the new prices start, then leaves it out of the profit projection. Including it cuts the gain substantially, and the margin target is missed.

The price increases may still be justified, but the paper needs correcting before the owners decide.

## 1. The risotto is the most profitable dish per pound of sales

Recalculating Table 1 confirms every margin figure:

| Dish | Margin |
|---|---|
| Fish and chips | 69% |
| Beef burger | 72% |
| Chicken curry | 75% |
| Sirloin steak | 60% |
| **Mushroom risotto** | **80%**, the highest |
| Specials | 64% |

Both the paper ("Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu") and the author's summary get this backwards. Also:
- **"Lowest sales" is a tie.** The risotto and the specials both sell 90 plates a week.
- **The replacement would probably earn less.** The proposed seasonal special has the same price but no cost given. If it performs like the current specials (64% margin), gross profit falls from £11.20 to about £8.96 a plate. That's **about £200 a week, or roughly £10,000 a year, less**.
- **The risotto may be the only vegetarian main.** Removing it could affect whether vegetarian guests, and the tables they book with, choose the restaurant. That matters for a business with a loyal local base.

**Recommendation:** keep the risotto, or replace it only with a dish costed at a similar margin.

## 2. The beef price rise isn't in the projection

Section 4 reports a **12% beef price rise from 1 April**, the same day the new prices start. Section 5.3 assumes food costs stay the same.

If all of the food cost of the burger and steak were beef, the rise would add:
- **Burger:** £4.20 → about £4.70 a plate, which is +£0.50 × 260 plates = about £131 a week.
- **Steak:** £10.40 → about £11.65 a plate, which is +£1.25 × 120 plates = about £150 a week.

That's **up to about £280 a week**. It's an upper bound, because buns, chips and sides aren't beef.

| | Weekly | Annual |
|---|---|---|
| Paper's projection | £810 | £42,120 |
| Less beef cost rise, worst case | −£281 | −£14,600 |
| **Revised** | **about £530–810** | **about £27,500–42,100** |

On the steak, the £2 price rise only partly covers about £1.25 of extra cost, so the steak's margin barely improves at all.

## 3. The 71% margin claim doesn't hold

The main-course margin can only be estimated, because the specials have no stated price. Using a plausible average of about £16 for specials:
- **The paper's 71%** is about right *only if* food costs stay the same and the risotto stays on the menu.
- **Including the beef rise,** the margin is about **69%**.
- **Also replacing the risotto** with a typical special brings it to about **68%**.

On those estimates, the changes as proposed **miss the 70% target**.

## 4. VAT may be missing from the figures

UK menu prices include 20% VAT. The margins and the £810 a week are calculated on the VAT-inclusive prices, so each £1 price rise actually brings in about **£0.83**. On the paper's own projection, that turns **£810 a week into about £675**, before the beef cost rise.

All the margins are also overstated on a net-of-VAT basis. Fish and chips, for example, is about 63% rather than 69%. That doesn't change the ranking of the dishes, but it does mean the 70% target should be checked against how the owners' accounts actually measure margin.

If the business already reports margins on VAT-inclusive prices, it should say so explicitly.

## 5. "Volumes hold" needs a stress test

The whole gain depends on volumes holding. It's worth showing how much volume each dish could lose before the price rise stops paying off. Compared with keeping the old prices *after* the beef rise:

| Dish | Volume loss that cancels the gain |
|---|---|
| Fish and chips | about 8% |
| Burger | about 9% |
| Steak | about 12% |

These aren't large margins of safety, and the supporting evidence is thin:
- **"The last price change in 2024 had no visible effect"** is anecdotal; no data are given.
- **60% repeat guests** cuts both ways: regulars are the guests most likely to notice a price rise.
- **Lunch's share is never quantified.** The paper says weekday lunch is "a small share," but only Friday and Saturday dinner is given as a share of sales.

## 6. Monitoring and other points

- **The monitoring baseline is seasonal.** Comparing April and May against January and February will probably show *higher* volumes anyway, because spring trade is normally stronger. That could hide a real fall caused by the price rise. Compare against April and May 2025 instead, or against how the dishes whose prices didn't change are selling.
- **"Six trading days a week"** in the recommendation contradicts Section 2, which says the restaurant is open Wednesday to Sunday, which is five days.
- **"Remain the value option."** After the increases, the restaurant is no longer the cheapest for any of the three dishes. Each one is above the lowest competitor price, although all are still below the midpoint (fish £17.50 against a £17.98 midpoint, burger £16.00 against £16.50, steak £28.00 against £29.50). That's competitive, but no longer the lowest.
- **Annualising over 52 weeks** assumes no closures. Check this against the actual trading calendar.

## 7. What's sound

- Two months of till data for every dish, with correct margin calculations.
- A useful competitor check, and price rises that genuinely stay below each midpoint.
- Correct price-rise arithmetic: £1 × 310 + £1 × 260 + £2 × 120 = £810, × 52 = £42,120.
- Raising prices is a reasonable response after 18 months without a change and with rising costs.
- Weekly monitoring by dish is the right approach.

## Recommended changes before the owners decide

1. **Correct the risotto analysis.** It has the highest margin. Keep it, or replace it only with a dish costed at a similar margin.
2. **Include the beef price rise** in the projection and the margin estimate. Consider a slightly higher steak price, which still has room below the competitor midpoint.
3. **State whether the figures include VAT,** and restate them consistently.
4. **Add the volume sensitivity,** showing the drop that would cancel the gain on each dish.
5. **Monitor against last year's April and May,** not January and February.
6. **Fix "six trading days."**

Corrected, the proposal would probably still recommend raising prices, but with a realistic gain of about £27,000–35,000 a year rather than £42,000, and without removing the most profitable dish on the menu.
